reference_title: Design and Construction of Continuous Flight Auger Piles
chapter_title: Description of Continuous Flight Auger Pile Types and Basic Mechanisms

sections.title: Introduction
sections.summary: CFA piles are drilled foundations installed in one continuous operation using a hollow-stem continuous flight auger. Grout or concrete is pumped through the hollow auger stem as the auger is withdrawn, replacing the soil column. Reinforcement is placed into the fluid grout immediately after auger withdrawal. Typical diameters are 300–900 mm (12–36 in.) and lengths up to 30 m (100 ft). Minimum center-to-center spacing is 3 to 5 pile diameters. CFA piles avoid casing or slurry but are limited to soil or very weak rock profiles.
sections.body:
CFA piles are a type of drilled foundation in which the pile is drilled to the final depth in one continuous process using a continuous flight auger. While the auger is drilled into the ground, the flights of the auger are filled with soil, providing lateral support and maintaining the stability of the hole. At the same time the auger is withdrawn from the hole, concrete or a sand/cement grout is placed by pumping through the hollow center of the auger pipe to the base of the auger. Simultaneous pumping of the grout or concrete and withdrawing of the auger provides continuous support of the hole. Reinforcement is placed into the hole filled with fluid concrete/grout immediately after withdrawal of the auger.

CFA piles are typically installed with diameters ranging from 0.3 to 0.9 m (12 to 36 in.) and lengths of up to 30 m (100 ft). In the United States, the practice has typically tended toward smaller piles having diameters of 0.3 to 0.6 m (12 to 24 in.); European practice tends toward larger diameters up to 1.5 m (60 in.). Typical minimum center-to-center spacing is 3 to 5 pile diameters. Reinforcement is often confined to the upper 10 to 15 m (33 to 50 ft) of the pile, though full-length reinforcement is used in some cases.

CFA piles differ from conventional drilled shafts in that casing or slurry to temporarily support the hole is avoided. Drilling in one continuous process is faster but requires higher torque. CFA piles are limited to soil or very weak rock profiles; they do not develop end-bearing in rock that cannot be penetrated with an auger. Compared to driven piles, CFA piles minimize noise and vibration, eliminate splices and cutoffs, and can eliminate soil heave (non-displacement types). Disadvantages include less reliable QA methods and generation of soil spoils requiring disposal.
key_points: Drilled in one continuous operation with hollow-stem auger; grout/concrete pumped through stem during withdrawal
Typical diameter: 300–900 mm (12–36 in.); length up to 30 m (100 ft); min spacing 3–5D
Reinforcement placed into fluid grout after auger withdrawal; typically limited to upper 10–15 m
No casing or slurry needed; limited to soil or very weak rock (cannot socket into hard rock)
Advantages: fast, low noise/vibration, no splices; disadvantages: less reliable QA, soil spoils

sections.title: Construction Sequence
sections.summary: CFA pile construction has four critical phases: (1) drilling — auger advanced to design depth while flights remain full of soil (balanced rotation/penetration to prevent soil mining); (2) grouting — grout pumped under pressure [1.0–1.7 MPa (150–250 psi) at auger top] immediately upon reaching tip depth, with overrun volume of 15–20% above theoretical pile volume required; (3) auger withdrawal — slow, smooth continuous pull with no or very slow rotation; and (4) reinforcement placement into fluid grout after clearing pile head. DD piles use a displacement tool that laterally densifies soil, avoiding mining in loose sands.
sections.body:
Drilling: The key to CFA pile installation is balancing the auger rotation rate with the penetration rate so that the auger flights remain filled with soil. If the auger turns too rapidly relative to penetration rate, the auger acts as an Archimedes pump and conveys soil to the surface. This over-rotation causes lateral decompression of the ground inside the hole, loosening of in-situ soil, and ground subsidence. The proper rate of penetration may be difficult to maintain in mixed soil profiles. Drilled Displacement (DD) piles use a center pipe with a displacement auger of larger diameter and a bulge/plug that forces soil laterally, avoiding soil mining and densifying surrounding soil.

Grouting: When the drilling stage is complete, the grouting stage must begin immediately. Grout is pumped under pressure [typically 1.0 to 1.7 MPa (150 to 250 psi) at the top of the auger]. The auger is first lifted 150 mm (6 in.), pressure is applied to expel the plug (blow the plug), and the auger is re-seated at the tip elevation before smooth withdrawal begins. The minimum pressure must exceed overburden pressure at the discharge point. An overrun in grout volume of about 15 to 20% above the theoretical pile volume is required. Grout must be pumped continuously; discontinuous withdrawal produces necks and bulges.

Auger withdrawal: The auger should be pulled with no rotation or very slow rotation in the direction of drilling. Static pull helps maintain pressure at the base. Volume per unit length must be monitored continuously. When the grout reaches the surface, pressure is vented and subsequent withdrawal relies on volume control.

Rebar: Reinforcement is placed into the fluid grout/concrete immediately after auger removal. Cages up to 10–15 m (33–50 ft) are typically feasible. A full-length central bar is often placed for continuity and tension resistance. Minimum cover of 75 mm (3 in.) is typical. Dry sandy soils dewater the grout rapidly and may require retarding admixtures or VMAs to maintain workability during cage installation.
key_points: Drilling: balance rotation/penetration to keep auger flights full and avoid soil mining (decompression, subsidence)
Grouting must begin immediately upon reaching tip depth — delay risks seizing the auger
Grout pressure: 1.0–1.7 MPa (150–250 psi) at auger top; must exceed overburden at discharge point
Auger lifted 150 mm (6 in.) to blow plug; re-seated at tip; then smoothly withdrawn with no or slow rotation
Required grout overrun: 15–20% above theoretical pile volume; continuous monitoring required
DD piles: displacement auger densifies surrounding soil, avoids mining in loose sands
Rebar: placed into fluid grout immediately after withdrawal; 75 mm min cover; VMAs may be needed in sandy soils
